topic: One-Variable Data: Distributions and Measures of Center and Spread
skills: Reading histograms, dot plots and box plots

lesson.intro: One-variable data questions hand you a small pile of numbers --- as a list, as a frequency table, as a dot plot, as a histogram, or as a box plot --- and ask what is typical about them (a measure of \emph{centre}) or how scattered they are (a measure of \emph{spread}). Every one of these questions is answered with arithmetic you already know; the work is in reading the display correctly and in knowing which of the mean, median, mode and range the question actually wants. Expect two or three of them on a Digital SAT.

blocks.title: The four measures
blocks.body: A \textbf{data set} is just a list of values. Four numbers summarise it.\\[4pt]The \textbf{mean} is the total of the values divided by how many values there are. The \textbf{median} is the middle value once the list is written in order --- and if there is an even number of values, it is the mean of the two middle ones. The \textbf{mode} is the value that appears most often. The \textbf{range} is the largest value minus the smallest value.\\[4pt]For the list $4$, $9$, $6$, $4$, $12$: the mean is $\frac{4+9+6+4+12}{5}=\frac{35}{5}=7$; ordered the list is $4,4,6,9,12$, so the median is $6$; the mode is $4$; the range is $12-4=8$.

blocks.title: Formulas you must know
blocks.body: $$\text{mean}=\frac{\text{sum of the values}}{\text{number of values}}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \text{sum}=\text{mean}\times\text{number of values}$$$$\text{range}=\text{maximum}-\text{minimum}\qquad \text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1$$The right-hand form of the mean formula is the one that solves ``working backwards'' questions: if you know a mean and a count, you know the total.

blocks.title: Reading a frequency table, dot plot or histogram
blocks.body: All three displays say the same thing: \emph{this value occurred this many times}. In a dot plot each dot is one data value; in a histogram or frequency table the height (or the tabulated frequency) tells you how many times that value occurred.\\[4pt]To find the \textbf{mean}, multiply each value by its frequency, add the products, and divide by the \emph{total frequency}:\;$\text{mean}=\dfrac{\sum(\text{value}\times\text{frequency})}{\sum \text{frequency}}$.\\[4pt]To find the \textbf{median}, first find the total frequency $N$. The median sits at position $\frac{N+1}{2}$ when $N$ is odd, and is the mean of positions $\frac{N}{2}$ and $\frac{N}{2}+1$ when $N$ is even. Run a running total of the frequencies from the left until you reach that position.

blocks.title: Three mistakes that are built into the answer choices
blocks.body: \textbf{1. Taking the median without sorting.} The middle entry of the list as printed is almost never the median. Write the list in order first --- every time.\\[4pt]\textbf{2. Averaging the frequencies instead of the values.} In a table with values $0,1,2,3,4$ and frequencies $4,7,5,3,1$, the mean is \emph{not} $\frac{20}{5}=4$ and it is \emph{not} $\frac{0+1+2+3+4}{5}=2$. It is $\frac{0(4)+1(7)+2(5)+3(3)+4(1)}{20}=\frac{30}{20}=1.5$.\\[4pt]\textbf{3. Confusing range with interquartile range.} The range uses the two whisker ends of a box plot; the IQR uses the two ends of the \emph{box}. They are different numbers and both appear among the choices.

blocks.title: Outliers: what moves and what does not
blocks.body: An \textbf{outlier} is a value far from the rest of the data. Because the mean is built from the total, one extreme value drags it a long way. The median only cares about position, so it barely shifts --- usually by one place in the ordered list.\\[4pt]So for the list $12,14,15,16,18$ (mean $15$, median $15$), adding the value $90$ gives a mean of $\frac{165}{6}=27.5$ but a median of only $15.5$. \textbf{Add a high outlier:} the mean jumps up, the median creeps up. \textbf{Remove a high outlier:} the mean drops sharply, the median drops slightly. The rule reverses in sign for a low outlier. This is why a strongly skewed data set has a mean pulled toward the long tail and a median that stays with the bulk of the data.

blocks.title: Standard deviation --- compared, never computed
blocks.body: Standard deviation measures how far a typical value sits from the mean. \textbf{The SAT never asks you to compute one.} Every standard-deviation question is a comparison, and it is decided by a single question: \emph{in which data set are the values packed more tightly around the mean?}\\[4pt]Tightly clustered values $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{smaller} standard deviation. Values spread far from the mean, or piled up at the two ends, $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{larger} standard deviation. Identical values give a standard deviation of exactly $0$.\\[4pt]Two facts worth memorising: equal means tell you \emph{nothing} about standard deviation, and adding a far-away outlier always increases it.

blocks.title: Calculator / strategy
blocks.body: \textbf{Sort first, always.} Ten seconds of sorting removes the single most common error on this topic.\\[4pt]\textbf{Work in totals.} ``The mean of $12$ numbers is $7$'' is really the statement ``the numbers add to $84$''. Convert every mean in the question into a total, do the arithmetic on the totals, and convert back at the end.\\[4pt]\textbf{Don't compute what you can see.} For a spread comparison, look at the picture. For a box plot, read the five marks off the axis --- minimum, $Q_1$, median, $Q_3$, maximum --- and answer from those five numbers alone.

blocks.title: Worked example 1 --- a frequency table
blocks.body:
\textit{The table shows the number of pets owned by each of $20$ households.}\\[3pt]\begin{center}\begin{tabular}{@{}cccccc@{}}\toprule
Pets & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4\\ \midrule
Households & 4 & 7 & 5 & 3 & 1\\ \bottomrule
\end{tabular}\end{center}\textit{(a) What is the mean number of pets? (b) What is the median?}\\[4pt]\textbf{(a)} Multiply each value by its frequency and add:
$0(4)+1(7)+2(5)+3(3)+4(1)=0+7+10+9+4=30$ pets in all. There are $4+7+5+3+1=20$ households, so the mean is $\frac{30}{20}=1.5$ pets.\\[4pt]\textbf{(b)} With $N=20$ values the median is the mean of the $10$th and $11$th values in order. Running totals: the first $4$ values are $0$; values $5$ through $11$ are $1$. So both the $10$th and the $11$th value are $1$, and the median is $1$.\\[4pt]Notice that $\frac{20}{5}=4$ (the mean of the frequencies) and $\frac{0+1+2+3+4}{5}=2$ (the mean of the listed values) are both wrong --- and both will be sitting in the answer choices.

blocks.title: Worked example 2 --- working backwards, and an outlier
blocks.body: \textit{The mean of nine numbers is $32$. A tenth number is added and the mean of all ten numbers becomes $38$. What is the tenth number?}\\[4pt]Turn both means into totals. Nine numbers with mean $32$ add to $9\times 32=288$. Ten numbers with mean $38$ add to $10\times 38=380$. The tenth number is therefore $380-288=92$.\\[4pt]That $92$ is an outlier: it sits far above a group averaging $32$. Consistent with the rule above, it pushed the mean up by $6$ --- while the median would have moved by at most half a place. If a follow-up question asked what happened to the standard deviation, the answer is that it increased, because a value that far from the mean makes the typical distance from the mean larger.

problems.stem: The high temperatures, in degrees Fahrenheit, recorded in a town on five days were $61$, $70$, $72$, $78$, and $84$. What is the mean of these five temperatures?
problems.solution: The mean is the total divided by the number of values, so it depends on every value in the list. Choice B, $72$, is the middle value of the ordered list --- that is the median, not the mean, and the two agree only by coincidence.
problems.verify:
vals = [61, 70, 72, 78, 84]
result = Rational(sum(vals), len(vals))

problems.stem: The numbers of books read last month by seven students were $5$, $2$, $9$, $4$, $7$, $3$, and $6$. What is the median number of books read?
problems.solution: The median is the middle value \emph{of the ordered list}. Choice A is the value sitting in the middle of the list as it was printed, which is the single most common error on this topic; choice D is simply the largest value.
steps: Write the values in increasing order: $2,3,4,5,6,7,9$.
There are $7$ values, so the median is the $4$th one, which is $5$.
problems.verify:
vals = sorted([5, 2, 9, 4, 7, 3, 6])
result = vals[3]

problems.stem: The masses, in grams, of six mineral samples were $12$, $19$, $7$, $15$, $22$, and $10$. What is the range of these masses, in grams?
problems.solution: The range measures spread, not centre: it is one subtraction, largest minus smallest. Nothing between the extremes affects it.
steps: The largest mass is $22$ and the smallest is $7$.
problems.verify:
vals = [12, 19, 7, 15, 22, 10]
result = max(vals) - min(vals)

problems.stem: A shoe store recorded the sizes of the eight pairs of shoes it sold in one hour: $8$, $9$, $7$, $9$, $10$, $8$, $9$, and $11$. What is the mode of these sizes?
problems.solution: The mode is the \emph{value} that occurs most often, not how often it occurs. Choice A is the number of times size $9$ appeared, and choice B is a size that appeared only twice.
steps: Count each size: $7$ appears once, $8$ twice, $9$ three times, $10$ once, $11$ once.
The size with the greatest count is $9$.

problems.skill: Reading histograms, dot plots and box plots
problems.stem: The dot plot shows the number of pets owned by each of $15$ families. What is the median number of pets?
problems.solution: Each dot is one family, so the dot plot is a list written vertically. With $15$ values the median is the $8$th, which you find by counting dots from the left. Choice A is the mode (the tallest stack) and choice C is the midpoint of the axis, neither of which is the median.
steps: There are $15$ dots, so the median is the $8$th value counting from the left.
Running totals: $2$ dots at $0$, then $5$ at $1$ (through the $7$th value), then $4$ at $2$.
problems.verify:
pairs = [[0, 2], [1, 5], [2, 4], [3, 2], [4, 1], [5, 1]]
vals = sorted(sum([[v] * f for v, f in pairs], []))
result = vals[7]

problems.stem: Over eight weeks, a runner ran $14$, $18$, $12$, $20$, $16$, $22$, $19$, and $15$ miles. What was the mean number of miles the runner ran per week?
problems.solution: ``Per week'' signals a mean: pool all the miles, then share them equally across the eight weeks.
problems.verify:
vals = [14, 18, 12, 20, 16, 22, 19, 15]
result = Rational(sum(vals), len(vals))

problems.skill: Reading histograms, dot plots and box plots
problems.stem: The box plot summarizes the ages, in years, of the trees in a small orchard. What is the median age of the trees?
problems.solution: A box plot shows five numbers: the two whisker ends are the minimum and maximum, the two ends of the box are $Q_1$ and $Q_3$, and the line inside the box is the median. Choices A, B and D are the minimum, $Q_1$ and $Q_3$.
steps: The line drawn inside the box marks the median.
That line sits at $24$ on the axis.
problems.verify: result = 24

problems.stem: The frequency table shows the number of siblings reported by each of $20$ students. What is the mean number of siblings per student?
problems.solution: A frequency table is a compressed list: the value $1$ really appears seven times. Multiply value by frequency before adding. Choice D is the mean of the frequencies, $\frac{20}{5}=4$, and choice C is the mean of the five listed values --- both ignore how often each value actually occurred.
problems.verify:
pairs = [[0, 4], [1, 7], [2, 5], [3, 3], [4, 1]]
result = Rational(sum([v * f for v, f in pairs]), sum([f for v, f in pairs]))

problems.stem: A biologist recorded the heights, in centimetres, of ten seedlings: $31$, $45$, $28$, $52$, $39$, $47$, $33$, $41$, $36$, and $50$. What is the median height?
problems.solution: With an even number of values there is no single middle value, so the median is the mean of the two middle ones \emph{after sorting}. Choice D is what you get by averaging the fifth and sixth entries of the unsorted list, $39$ and $47$.
steps: With $10$ values the median is the mean of the $5$th and $6$th: $\frac{39+41}{2}=40$.
problems.verify:
vals = sorted([31, 45, 28, 52, 39, 47, 33, 41, 36, 50])
result = Rational(vals[4] + vals[5], 2)

problems.stem: The mean of five test scores is $84$. Four of the scores are $78$, $91$, $85$, and $80$. What is the fifth score?
problems.solution: Convert the mean into a total. Knowing that the five scores must add to $420$ turns the question into one subtraction. Choice A is the mean of the four given scores and choice B assumes the missing score equals the mean.
steps: Five scores with mean $84$ must total $5\times 84=420$.

problems.stem: A data set consists of the nine values $12$, $14$, $15$, $16$, $18$, $19$, $21$, $23$, and $24$. The value $90$ is then added to the data set. Which of the following best describes the effect of adding $90$?
choices: The mean and the median increase by the same amount.
The median increases by more than the mean does.
The mean increases and the median decreases.
The mean increases by much more than the median does.
problems.solution: The mean is built from the total, so one huge value drags it a long way; the median only counts positions, so it slides by half a place. Here the mean goes from $18$ to $25.2$ while the median goes from $18$ to $18.5$.
steps: Original: total $=162$, so the mean is $\frac{162}{9}=18$; the median is the $5$th value, $18$.
After adding $90$: total $=252$, so the mean is $\frac{252}{10}=25.2$.
The mean rose by $7.2$; the median rose by $0.5$.
problems.verify: result = "The mean increases by much more than the median does."

problems.skill: Reading histograms, dot plots and box plots
problems.stem: The dot plot shows the scores of $20$ students on a $10$-point quiz. What is the mean score?
problems.solution: A dot plot is a frequency table drawn with dots, so the mean is found the same way: value times frequency, added, then divided by the number of dots --- not by the number of columns.
problems.verify:
pairs = [[6, 1], [7, 3], [8, 6], [9, 5], [10, 5]]
result = Rational(sum([v * f for v, f in pairs]), sum([f for v, f in pairs]))

problems.stem: Data set $X$ consists of the values $20$, $21$, $22$, $23$, and $24$. Data set $Y$ consists of the values $12$, $17$, $22$, $27$, and $32$. Each data set has a mean of $22$. Which of the following is true about the standard deviations of the two data sets?
choices: Data set $X$ has the larger standard deviation, because its values are closer to the mean.
The standard deviations are equal, because the two data sets have the same mean.
The standard deviations are equal, because the two data sets have the same number of values.
Data set $Y$ has the larger standard deviation, because its values are farther from the mean.
problems.solution: Standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean, so compare how tightly the values cluster. The values of $X$ are within $2$ of $22$; the values of $Y$ reach $10$ away. Equal means say nothing at all about spread, which rules out choices B and C.
steps: Both data sets have mean $22$, so compare distances from $22$.
Data set $X$: distances $2,1,0,1,2$. Data set $Y$: distances $10,5,0,5,10$.
The values of $Y$ sit farther from the mean, so $Y$ has the larger standard deviation.
problems.verify: result = "Data set $Y$ has the larger standard deviation, because its values are farther from the mean."

problems.skill: Reading histograms, dot plots and box plots
problems.stem: The box plot summarizes the number of minutes that each of $40$ commuters waited for a train. What is the interquartile range of the wait times, in minutes?
problems.solution: The interquartile range is the width of the \emph{box}, $Q_3-Q_1$; the range is the distance between the whisker ends. Choice D, $30-4=26$, is the range --- the distractor this question is built around.
problems.verify: result = 22 - 10

problems.stem: The mean of six numbers is $15$. When one of the numbers is removed, the mean of the remaining five numbers is $16$. What is the value of the number that was removed?
problems.solution: Two means, two totals. The removed number is the difference between them --- and notice that removing a number \emph{raised} the mean, so the number removed had to be below the original mean.

problems.skill: Reading histograms, dot plots and box plots
problems.stem: The histogram shows the number of goals scored in each of $20$ soccer games. What is the mean number of goals per game?
problems.solution: Read each bar as a value with a frequency, then take a weighted mean. Choice C, $4$, is the mean of the five bar heights, $\frac{20}{5}$; choice D is the tallest bar. Neither uses the goal values at all.
problems.verify:
pairs = [[0, 3], [1, 5], [2, 7], [3, 4], [4, 1]]
result = Rational(sum([v * f for v, f in pairs]), sum([f for v, f in pairs]))

problems.stem: In the frequency table shown, the value $4$ occurs $x$ times. The mean of all the data is $3.4$. What is the value of $x$?
problems.solution: Write the mean formula with $x$ in both the numerator and the denominator, then clear the fraction. The unknown frequency changes the total \emph{and} the count, which is why it appears twice.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
result = solve(Eq(49 + 4*x, Rational(17, 5) * (16 + x)), x)[0]

problems.stem: The dot plots show two data sets, each consisting of $10$ values with a mean of $6$. Which data set has the larger standard deviation, and why?
choices: Data set $P$, because more of its values are far from the mean.
Data set $P$, because its values are more tightly clustered.
Neither, because the two data sets have the same mean.
Data set $Q$, because more of its values are far from the mean.
problems.solution: With the means equal, the comparison is entirely about clustering. Data set $P$ piles up at $6$; data set $Q$ piles up at $4$ and $8$, so a typical value of $Q$ sits $2$ away from the mean while a typical value of $P$ sits well under $1$ away.
steps: Both data sets have mean $6$, so compare distances from $6$.
In $P$ most values are at $6$ itself, and none is more than $2$ away with only one at each end.
In $Q$ eight of the ten values are $2$ away from the mean.
$Q$ has the larger typical distance from the mean, so it has the larger standard deviation.
problems.verify: result = "Data set $Q$, because more of its values are far from the mean."

problems.stem: The yearly salaries, in thousands of dollars, of the eight employees at a small company are $32$, $35$, $36$, $38$, $40$, $42$, $45$, and $180$. The salary of $180$ is removed from the data set. Which of the following describes the change in the mean and in the median?
choices: The mean decreases by about $18$ and the median decreases by $1$.
The mean decreases by $1$ and the median decreases by about $18$.
The mean and the median each decrease by about $18$.
The mean decreases and the median is unchanged.
problems.solution: This is the outlier rule in numbers: the mean falls from $56$ to about $38.3$, a drop of roughly $18$, while the median falls only from $39$ to $38$. The median is resistant to outliers precisely because it depends on position rather than on size.
steps: The mean falls by about $18$; the median falls by $1$.
problems.verify: result = "The mean decreases by about $18$ and the median decreases by $1$."

problems.stem: In one class of $24$ students, the mean score on a test was $78$. In a second class of $16$ students, the mean score on the same test was $88$. What is the mean score of all $40$ students?
problems.solution: You cannot average two means directly unless the groups are the same size --- $\frac{78+88}{2}=83$ is wrong here. Rebuild both totals, add them, and divide by the combined count so the larger class carries more weight.
problems.verify: result = Rational(24 * 78 + 16 * 88, 40)

problems.stem: The table shows the number of days absent for each of the $35$ students in a class. What is the median number of days absent?
problems.solution: Find the total frequency first: with $35$ values the median is the $18$th, so run a cumulative total until you pass $18$. Choice B is the mode --- the value with the largest frequency --- and choice D is the median of the frequency column, both of which answer a question that was not asked.
steps: Total students: $6+9+8+7+5=35$, so the median is the $18$th value in order.
Cumulative totals: $6$ students at $0$ day, $15$ through $1$ day, $23$ through $2$ days.
The $18$th value falls in the $2$-day group, so the median is $2$.
problems.verify:
pairs = [[0, 6], [1, 9], [2, 8], [3, 7], [4, 5]]
vals = sorted(sum([[v] * f for v, f in pairs], []))
result = vals[17]

problems.stem: The mean of $12$ numbers is $7$. A thirteenth number is added to the data set, and the mean of all $13$ numbers is $8$. What is the thirteenth number?
problems.solution: Raising the mean of $12$ numbers by $1$ requires enough extra to lift all thirteen values, not just one: $13$ extra units on top of the new value's own share. Choice A assumes the new number simply equals the new mean, which would have left the mean unchanged at $7$.

problems.stem: The prices, in dollars, of eight items sold at a shop are $14$, $9$, $21$, $16$, $12$, $18$, $25$, and $11$. What is the median price, in dollars?
problems.solution: An even count means the median is the average of the two middle values of the sorted list. Choices A and D are those two middle values on their own, and choice C is the mean.
steps: With $8$ values the median is the mean of the $4$th and $5$th: $\frac{14+16}{2}=15$.
problems.verify:
vals = sorted([14, 9, 21, 16, 12, 18, 25, 11])
result = Rational(vals[3] + vals[4], 2)

problems.stem: The table shows the number of children in each of $50$ households in a neighbourhood. What is the mode of the number of children per household?
problems.solution: In a frequency table the mode is the value in the left column that carries the largest frequency, not the frequency itself. Choice D, $19$, is how many households had that number of children.
steps: The largest frequency in the table is $19$.
That frequency belongs to the value $2$, so the mode is $2$ children.

problems.skill: Reading histograms, dot plots and box plots
problems.stem: The dot plot shows the number of questions answered correctly by each of $12$ students on a short test. What is the range of the number of correct answers?
problems.solution: The range is a subtraction of the two extreme \emph{values}, and on a dot plot those are the leftmost and rightmost columns that actually contain dots. Choice B counts the columns, choice C reports the largest value alone, and choice D counts the dots.
steps: The leftmost dot is above $3$ and the rightmost dot is above $9$.
problems.verify:
pairs = [[3, 1], [4, 2], [5, 3], [6, 2], [7, 2], [8, 1], [9, 1]]
vals = sorted(sum([[v] * f for v, f in pairs], []))
result = max(vals) - min(vals)

problems.skill: Reading histograms, dot plots and box plots
problems.stem: The box plot summarizes the masses, in kilograms, of the dogs treated at a clinic in one week. What is the value of the third quartile, $Q_3$?
problems.solution: $Q_3$ is the right-hand edge of the box: a quarter of the data lies above it. Choice A is $Q_1$ (the left edge), choice B is the median (the line inside), and choice C is the midpoint of the two whisker ends, which no box plot marks.
steps: The right-hand edge of the box is at $58$, so $Q_3=58$.
problems.verify: result = 58

problems.stem: The rainfall, in inches, recorded in a town in each of six months was $2.4$, $3.1$, $1.8$, $2.9$, $3.6$, and $4.2$. What was the mean monthly rainfall, in inches?
problems.solution: Decimals change nothing about the method: add every value, then divide by how many values there are.
problems.verify:
vals = [Rational(24,10), Rational(31,10), Rational(18,10), Rational(29,10), Rational(36,10), Rational(42,10)]
result = Rational(sum(vals), len(vals))

problems.stem: Data set $A$ consists of the five values $50$, $50$, $50$, $50$, and $50$. Data set $B$ consists of the five values $46$, $48$, $50$, $52$, and $54$. Which data set has the greater standard deviation, and why?
choices: Data set $A$, because all of its values are equal to the mean.
Data set $A$, because it has the greater mean.
They have the same standard deviation, because they have the same mean.
Data set $B$, because its values vary while those of data set $A$ do not.
problems.solution: Standard deviation is the typical distance from the mean. In data set $A$ every value \emph{is} the mean, so that distance is $0$ --- the smallest a standard deviation can ever be. Any variation at all beats it.
steps: Both data sets have a mean of $50$.
In data set $A$ every value equals the mean, so the standard deviation is $0$.
Data set $B$ has values up to $4$ away from the mean, so its standard deviation is greater than $0$.
problems.verify: result = "Data set $B$, because its values vary while those of data set $A$ do not."

problems.stem: The table shows the number of correct answers, out of $4$, for each of $15$ students on a short quiz. What is the median number of correct answers?
problems.solution: With $15$ values the median is the $8$th in order; a cumulative count of the frequencies locates it. Choice B is the mode, choice C is the largest frequency, and choice D is the number of students.
steps: Total students: $2+3+4+6=15$, so the median is the $8$th value.
Cumulative totals: $2$ through score $1$, $5$ through score $2$, $9$ through score $3$.
The $8$th value falls in the score-$3$ group, so the median is $3$.
problems.verify:
pairs = [[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4], [4, 6]]
vals = sorted(sum([[v] * f for v, f in pairs], []))
result = vals[7]

problems.stem: The table shows the number of cars owned by each of $25$ families. What is the mean number of cars per family?
problems.solution: Weight each value by its frequency. Choice D is the mean of the frequencies ($\frac{25}{5}=5$), choice C is the mean of the five listed values, and choice A is the median. Only choice B uses both columns of the table.
problems.verify:
pairs = [[0, 5], [1, 8], [2, 6], [3, 4], [4, 2]]
result = Rational(sum([v * f for v, f in pairs]), sum([f for v, f in pairs]))

problems.stem: A data set consists of the six values $4$, $9$, $11$, $x$, $17$, and $20$, listed in increasing order. The median of the data set is $13$. What is the value of $x$?
problems.solution: For six values the median is the average of the third and fourth, so the stated median gives an equation in $x$ rather than a value you can read off. The answer, $15$, does lie between $11$ and $17$, so the list really is in increasing order.
steps: With $6$ values the median is the mean of the $3$rd and $4$th values: $\frac{11+x}{2}$.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
result = solve(Eq(Rational(1, 2) * (11 + x), 13), x)[0]

problems.stem: A data set of $10$ numbers has a mean of $46$. One value of $23$ is replaced by $63$, and no other value is changed. What is the mean of the new data set?
problems.solution: Only the total changes, and it changes by $63-23=40$. That extra $40$ is then shared among all ten values, raising the mean by $4$. Choice D adds the whole $40$ to the mean without dividing.
steps: Replacing $23$ by $63$ increases the total by $63-23=40$, giving $500$.
There are still $10$ values, so the new mean is $\frac{500}{10}=50$.
problems.verify: result = Rational(10 * 46 - 23 + 63, 10)

problems.skill: Reading histograms, dot plots and box plots
problems.stem: The histogram shows the number of siblings of each of $30$ students. What is the median number of siblings?
problems.solution: Convert the histogram to a running count. With $30$ values the median is the average of the $15$th and $16$th, and both land in the same bar, so no averaging is actually needed. Choice A is the mode (the tallest bar) and choice D is the largest value on the axis.
steps: Total students: $4+9+7+5+3+2=30$, so the median averages the $15$th and $16$th values.
Cumulative totals: $4$ through $0$ siblings, $13$ through $1$, $20$ through $2$.
Both the $15$th and the $16$th value are $2$, so the median is $2$.
problems.verify:
pairs = [[0, 4], [1, 9], [2, 7], [3, 5], [4, 3], [5, 2]]
vals = sorted(sum([[v] * f for v, f in pairs], []))
result = Rational(vals[14] + vals[15], 2)

problems.skill: Reading histograms, dot plots and box plots
problems.stem: The box plots summarize the test scores of the students in class $A$ and class $B$. Which of the following statements is true?
choices: The two classes have the same median, and class $A$ has the larger interquartile range.
Class $B$ has the larger median and the larger interquartile range.
The two classes have the same median, and class $B$ has the larger range.
Class $A$ has the larger median, and the two classes have the same range.
problems.solution: Read all five marks off each plot before judging. The two medians coincide at $76$, but class $A$'s box is twice as wide ($84-68=16$ against $80-72=8$), and its whiskers are wider too ($95-55=40$ against $90-62=28$), so class $A$ is the more spread out of the two.
problems.verify: result = "The two classes have the same median, and class $A$ has the larger interquartile range."

problems.stem: The $18$ students in a class have a mean height of $62$ inches. Two new students, of heights $70$ inches and $74$ inches, join the class. What is the mean height, in inches, of the $20$ students?
problems.solution: Averaging the old mean with the mean of the two newcomers gives $67$, choice D --- but that treats two students as though they outweighed eighteen. Work with totals so the group sizes are respected.
steps: The original total height is $18\times 62=1116$ inches.
Adding the two new students gives $1116+70+74=1260$ inches.
problems.verify: result = Rational(18 * 62 + 70 + 74, 20)

problems.stem: The numbers of customers a cashier served during each of eight hours were $3$, $7$, $8$, $12$, $13$, $15$, $18$, and $25$. What is the interquartile range of these numbers?
problems.solution: Split the ordered list in half and take the median of each half: $Q_1$ from the lower four values, $Q_3$ from the upper four. The IQR describes the middle half of the data, so the extreme value $25$ has no effect on it --- unlike the range, which would be $22$.
steps: The eight values are already in order, so split them into two halves of four.
problems.verify:
vals = sorted([3, 7, 8, 12, 13, 15, 18, 25])
q1 = Rational(vals[1] + vals[2], 2)
q3 = Rational(vals[5] + vals[6], 2)
result = q3 - q1

problems.stem: A data set consists of the seven values $4$, $6$, $7$, $9$, $10$, $12$, and $40$. The value $40$ is removed from the data set. Which of the following describes the change in the mean and in the median?
choices: The median decreases by more than the mean does.
The mean is unchanged and the median decreases.
Both the mean and the median increase.
The mean decreases by more than the median does.
problems.solution: Removing a high outlier pulls the total down hard, so the mean falls from about $12.6$ to $8$; the median only shifts from $9$ to $8$ because it merely moves half a place in the ordered list.
steps: Original mean: $\frac{88}{7}\approx 12.6$; original median: the $4$th value, $9$.
After removal the six values total $48$, so the mean is $\frac{48}{6}=8$.
The mean fell by about $4.6$; the median fell by $1$.
problems.verify: result = "The mean decreases by more than the median does."

problems.stem: The mean of seven numbers is $24$. Two of the numbers, $15$ and $28$, are removed from the data set. What is the mean of the remaining five numbers?
problems.solution: Totals again: subtract the two removed values from the original total, then divide by the new count of five. Because the two removed numbers averaged only $21.5$ --- below $24$ --- the mean of what is left has to rise.
steps: Removing $15$ and $28$ leaves a total of $168-43=125$.
Five numbers remain, so the mean is $\frac{125}{5}=25$.
problems.verify: result = Rational(7 * 24 - 15 - 28, 5)

problems.stem: Two data sets each consist of $20$ values with a mean of $50$. In data set $R$, $16$ of the values are between $48$ and $52$. In data set $S$, $16$ of the values are less than $40$ or greater than $60$. Which of the following statements is true?
choices: Data set $R$ has the larger standard deviation, because more of its values are near $50$.
The standard deviations are equal, because the means are equal.
The standard deviations cannot be compared without calculating each one.
Data set $S$ has the larger standard deviation, because more of its values are far from $50$.
problems.solution: You are never asked to compute a standard deviation on this test, and here you do not need to: with equal means, the data set whose values sit farther from that mean has the larger standard deviation. Choice C states the opposite of how the SAT treats this topic.
steps: Both data sets have the same mean, $50$, so compare distances from $50$.
In $R$, most values are within $2$ of the mean.
In $S$, most values are more than $10$ from the mean.
A larger typical distance from the mean means a larger standard deviation, so $S$ is larger.
problems.verify: result = "Data set $S$ has the larger standard deviation, because more of its values are far from $50$."

problems.stem: The mean of nine numbers is $15$. Each of the nine numbers is increased by $4$, and each result is then doubled. What is the mean of the nine new numbers?
problems.solution: Doing the same operations to every value does the same operations to the mean, but the \emph{order} matters: increase first, then double. Choice B doubles before adding, which reverses the instructions.
steps: Adding $4$ to every value adds $4$ to the mean: $15+4=19$.
Doubling every value doubles the mean: $2\times 19=38$.
problems.verify: result = 2 * (15 + 4)

problems.stem: The table shows the scores of the $40$ students who took a quiz. What is the median score?
problems.solution: The median is a position, not an average: with $40$ scores it lies between the $20$th and the $21$st, and both of those fall in the $80$ group. Choice B is the mean, $79.75$, which is pulled below the median by the six low scores of $70$.
steps: Total students: $6+9+11+9+5=40$, so the median averages the $20$th and $21$st scores.
Cumulative totals: $6$ through score $70$, $15$ through $75$, $26$ through $80$.
Both the $20$th and the $21$st score are $80$, so the median is $80$.
problems.verify:
pairs = [[70, 6], [75, 9], [80, 11], [85, 9], [90, 5]]
vals = sorted(sum([[v] * f for v, f in pairs], []))
result = Rational(vals[19] + vals[20], 2)

problems.stem: A data set consists of $15$ values, each between $40$ and $60$. A new value of $200$ is then added to the data set. Compared with the original data set, which of the following must be true of the new data set?
choices: Both the mean and the standard deviation are larger.
The mean is larger and the standard deviation is smaller.
The mean is unchanged and the standard deviation is larger.
The median increases by more than the mean does.
problems.solution: A value far above every other value raises the total, so the mean rises; and it sits an enormous distance from the mean, so the typical distance from the mean --- the standard deviation --- rises as well. The median, by contrast, moves at most half a place, so it cannot rise by more than the mean does.
steps: The new value is larger than every existing value, so the total rises and the mean rises.
The new value lies far from the mean, so it increases the typical distance from the mean.
Therefore both the mean and the standard deviation are larger.
problems.verify: result = "Both the mean and the standard deviation are larger."

problems.stem: A class of $30$ students took a test. The $12$ students in group A had a mean score of $85$, and the class as a whole had a mean score of $79$. What was the mean score of the other $18$ students?
problems.solution: The whole-class total splits into the two group totals. Subtracting group A's total leaves the other group's total, which then divides by $18$. The answer must fall below $79$, since group A scored above the class mean.
problems.verify: result = Rational(30 * 79 - 12 * 85, 18)

problems.stem: A data set of $20$ values has a mean of $42$. When two of the values are removed, the mean of the remaining $18$ values is $40$. What is the mean of the two values that were removed?
problems.solution: Removing two values dropped the mean of eighteen numbers by $2$, which means those two values carried $18\times 2=36$ units of surplus on top of their own share. Choice A, the average of the two stated means, ignores the group sizes entirely.
problems.verify: result = Rational(20 * 42 - 18 * 40, 2)
